articles.title: The surprising science of what pain is and why it hurts
articles.author: Dave Newell, Professor of Integrated Musculoskeletal Care and Head of the Centre of Pain and Active Inference Research, Health Sciences University
paras: When you step into an ice-cold lake, it would be nice if your body warned you about possible harm with a polite message: “Your feet may be at risk. Would you kindly consider stepping out?”

Instead, your feet hurt. A lot. Your attention narrows and getting out becomes an urgent priority. Friends’ promises of fun suddenly matter much less. Why does information about possible bodily harm feel so unpleasant? Why can’t we register the danger as calmly as we take in the lakeside trees?
Part of the answer begins with another question: what is perception for?

Perception helps living things navigate the world: finding food, avoiding danger and maintaining a healthy body. All of this helps us survive. But how does a nervous system figure out what is happening and what to do next?

We seem to experience the world directly: the lake, the trees, our friends wondering why we’re making such a hasty exit. But the brain receives neither light nor sound directly. Instead, information from your eyes, ears, skin and internal organs reaches it through signals that include brief electrical impulses called “action potentials”. These signals carry no labels explaining what they mean. Yet you experience trees, voices and freezing feet.

Predictive theories of perception offer a counterintuitive explanation. They propose that your nervous system uses experience to predict, or make educated guesses about, what incoming sensory information means. Sensory signals are then used to check those predictions and revise them when they do not fit.

In this account, experience emerges from an ongoing exchange between predictions and sensory information. The world does not simply pour in through our senses. The nervous system helps construct our experience while continually checking it against signals from the world and body.

This educated guessing is called inference: drawing conclusions from incomplete information. Through experience, the nervous system learns patterns, sometimes called models, that help it anticipate what sensations might come next. You do not consult these patterns consciously. They are at work as you read, recognise a voice or feel painfully cold feet.

We usually assume that something acts on our senses first, followed by a sensation: the icy lake bathes your skin and then your feet feel cold and hurt. However, predictive accounts of pain suggest that unconscious interpretation helps shape the feeling itself. You do not first experience electrical signals and then give them meaning. What you feel may depend partly on how your nervous system interprets those signals at that moment.

There is evidence that expectations influence pain. In one experiment involving ten volunteers, researchers applied painful heat to their legs. When participants expected less intense heat than they actually received, they rated the same heat about 28% less painful. Brain scans also showed reduced activity in regions involved in processing pain. This demonstrates an effect of expectation, although it does not establish that predictive processing fully explains pain.
These predictions are not a conscious decision about whether something should hurt. Both information from the body and learned expectations matter; neither alone determines the experience.

A related framework, called “active inference”, links perception with action: what we feel influences how we act, and how we act changes what we experience. Living things do not just update predictions. They act to change what happens next, including the next set of information their senses receive.

In the lake, pain makes a possible threat feel urgent and prompts protective action. Getting out changes the signals reaching your nervous system. Feeling cold, feeling pain and wanting to escape are connected parts of a response aimed at protecting your body.

Sensory nerves also detect potentially damaging conditions, such as extreme cold. This process is called nociception. It provides important information, but it is not identical to pain, the unpleasant experience itself. The nervous system also draws on previous experience, expectations and circumstances when interpreting that information.
This helps explain why the intensity of pain does not necessarily correspond to the extent of tissue damage. Pain can persist without continuing injury.

Consider persistent back pain. Someone who has repeatedly felt pain when bending may anticipate it and move cautiously. Avoiding bending may bring relief, but also limit opportunities to learn whether movement has become safer or more manageable. Research links fear of movement with persistent back pain, although the evidence is uncertain.

One of us (Michael Thacker) and colleagues have proposed that active inference could help explain how past experiences shape feelings and actions. This is only one possible contributor to persistent pain, which can also involve ongoing tissue injury or damage to nerves. It does not imply that people consciously think themselves into pain.

So why does pain hurt? Active inference suggests that unpleasantness helps make a possible threat important enough to demand protection. But protection is not always useful. Pain can persist without continuing damage, and actions intended to protect us can sometimes become disabling. The theory suggests what unpleasantness might achieve, although it has not fully explained how the feeling itself arises.

Predictive theories still need further testing, particularly to establish whether they improve care. Their hopeful suggestion is that pain might be better understood through the relationship between the body, experience, action and circumstances, without ever doubting that the suffering of people with persistent pain is real.

articles.title: Microbes at the end of the earth: Antarctica’s hidden biodiversity
articles.author: Caray A Walker, Senior Lecturer in Microbiology, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: When we think about Antarctica, many people imagine penguins, seals and whales. However, the majority of Antarctica’s scientific wonders cannot be seen without a microscope. These microbial communities form the foundation of Antarctic ecosystems yet remain largely invisible to most visitors.

Recent research published in PNAS showed that some microbes living in Antarctic soils appear to exist nowhere else on Earth. This challenges scientists’ long-held belief that microbes are easily dispersed and therefore found everywhere.

Antarctica is one of the Earth’s most isolated and harsh environments. Its organisms have to deal with extreme cold, dryness, intense UV radiation and limited nutrients, creating selective pressures unique to the continent. Soil temperatures can range from around 8˚C during the summer to below -25˚C in winter while air temperatures can fall below -40˚C. Rapid temperature fluctuations are common, which creates particularly challenging conditions for life.

While extreme cold also occurs in the Arctic, it is the historical geographical isolation that characterises evolution to the cold in the Antarctic. Antarctic species have been effectively isolated in the cold from the rest of the planet by the circumpolar current for 10-15 million years, whereas the Arctic is still highly connected to other continents and has been cold for only around 1.5 million years.

The researchers studied strains of the bacterium Arthrobacter from Antarctica and compared them with samples from other cold and dry environments, such as the Atacama Desert, Svalbard and the Tibetan Plateau. They found distinct Antarctic strains that seem to have evolved in isolation on the continent, suggesting Antarctica’s conditions have allowed unique microbial communities to develop over long periods.

The fact that Antarctica may be home to organisms found nowhere else raises important questions about evolution, conservation and biotechnology – and particularly how we can preserve such cold-adapted biodiversity in a warming world.
These microbes are not simply biological curiosities. They play a fundamental role in nutrient cycling and form the base of Antarctic food webs.

Antarctic organisms have evolved remarkable biological solutions to survive conditions that would be destructive to other organisms. They can withstand air temperatures often permanently well below 0°C, extreme desiccation in soils with no annual rainfall and extended exposure to high levels of UV-B in the Antarctic summer.

The same adaptations that allow Antarctic organisms to survive may have major practical applications. For instance, our own research, published in 2025, examined the antimicrobial potential of bacteria cultured from eight Antarctic marine invertebrate species, such as sea cucumbers, sea stars and anemones. We found that two strains of these bacteria (Psychrobacter and Pseudomonas) could inhibit the growth of microorganisms of clinical importance such as epidemic methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Micrococcus luteus,and Candida albicans _in laboratory tests.

As well as Antarctica being a potential source of new drugs and enzymes, its isolated geographical location means that it is a protected ecosystem and is often referred to as “the last great wilderness”. Human activities like tourism and increased scientific activity can risk introducing non-native microorganisms and diseases to Antarctic communities, which have evolved in relative isolation and may lack resilience against introduced organisms.

Recent research from our laboratory monitored antimicrobial resistance (AMR) caused by humans. Affecting both animals and humans, antimicrobial resistance is a global issue that means some drugs which are used to medicate infections no longer work, leaving some infections untreatable. Our research looked specifically at the extent of AMR around the Rothera Research Station (operated by the UK) on the Antarctic Peninsula.
Overall, our study suggests that treated wastewater has only a limited effect on surrounding marine microbial communities.

However, when we grew these bacteria in our lab we saw that the bacteria easily adapted to warmer temperatures, which suggests rising temperatures worldwide could change these microbes. This means they may no longer yield some of the potential products we can take advantage of, like cold-adapted enzymes, which work efficiently at room temperature. The vast majority of industrial and chemical reactions using enzymes often require high amounts of energy to make them work. If we could identify “cold-adapted” versions of these enzymes and introduce them into large-scale production processes, we would reduce our energy requirements and move towards net zero emissions.

Antarctic microbes may not attract the same public attention as penguins, seals or whales but they represent some of the continent’s most distinctive biodiversity. They also drive key ecosystem processes that those popular animals depend upon. Therefore changes in microbial biodiversity may have consequences that extend far beyond the microbes themselves.
Protecting this largely unseen biodiversity from climate change and increasing human activities is essential if we are to preserve both its ecological value and its future potential.

articles.title: Medieval monks were early ecologists and left a wealth of knowledge for later generations of gardeners
articles.author: Giles Gasper, Professor in High Medieval History, Durham University
paras: For whatever the land you possess, whether it be where sand And gravel lie barren and dead, or where fruits grow heavy In rich moist ground; whether high on a steep hillside, Easy ground in the plain or rough among sloping valleys - Whereever it is, your land cannot fail to produce Its native plants…
These words come the Hortulus: The Little Garden written by Wahlafrid Strabo (c. 808-849), who was a Benedictine monk from the monastery of Reichnau on an island in Lake Constance.

The 9th-century Hortulus is considered one of the most important European historical documents on gardening and plants, combining practical advice with its poetry. It continues to inspire modern gardeners in planting and design. The writings offer a tour of the monastery garden and the qualities of its plants. Twenty-nine plants are named, from Indian pepper to grapes, nettle, pennyroyal and peach. For the most part these are medicinal, though Wahlafrid includes some culinary observations, and a final detail about the rose as a source of soothing oil and symbol of the Virgin Mary.
The descriptions of the fresh and delightful taste of melon and gourds (bottle gourd or calabash) sit alongside longer discussion of the use and preparation of herbs and vegetables for health.

As a flavour of the way in which these observations were made, take the plant Southernwood (Aretemisia Abrotanum), not commonly known these days but common enough in the medieval period. Strabo notes that: “It has power against fevers, banishes stitch, and if your limbs ache with the elusive and mysterious pain of gout, it will bring relief.”
Other instructions show how monks used plants as medicine including mixing fennel-root with wine to relieve a rasping cough, and the use of betony as a treatment for a septic wound.

Around 350 years later, in his large work On the Nature of Things, Alexander Neckham, a English Augustinian canon (so, not strictly a monk), wrote a description of a garden, probably recalling his days as a scholar in Paris. His list includes parsley, coriander, savory, cress, sorrel, ponlions, leeks, garlic and purslane, medlars, quinces and citrus fruits. He notes a number of herbs (spices) which do not grow in Europe, including ginger, clove, zedoary and myrrh. Neckham emphasises the importance of hard work in the garden, but also the importance of studying plants and their uses.

This combination of book learning, community knowledge and experience can be found in what is known as “the Herbal”, which refers to historical writings on the science and health qualities of plants. These were copied, and added to, by hand. One of the earliest is On Medical Matters compiled by Dioscorides (c.40-c.90 AD), written in Greek and translated into Latin and Arabic.
This became a standard reference text, some with illustrations, in medieval Europe. Much of the focus lies on the medicinal usage of herbs, but also uses in cooking.
The plant lore of the monastic library might be supplemented by longer traditions of Roman science, for example the Natural History of Pliny the Elder (d.79 AD).

And the tradition continued with authors such as Henry of Huntingdon, a 12-century archdeacon, whose work the English Garden deals with six times the number of plants as Strabo, in a more elaborate literary tour of the garden and its plots.
Works by four other key botanists, Isidore, Bede, Macer, and Dioscorides, are to be found in the mid-12th century catalogue of the monastic library at Durham Cathedral Priory.

Then as now, health and eating were considered closely related. Most monasteries kept gardens. For instance, on the famous ninth-century architectural plan of an idealised monastery layout, known as the Plan of St Gall, a main kitchen garden as well as an orchard are shown.

Knowledge of plant lore was passed down through the centuries by monks. This was part of a wider monastic approach to the natural environment, which has some resonance with gardening movements of today, by combining spirituality and mental health with growing and eating plants.

The 12th-century theologian William of St Thierry describes shady woodland, recognising the idea of spirituality gained from the natural world. He wrote that the “silent valley spoke to them of the simplicity and humility in the buildings, mirroring the simplicity and humility of those living there”.

Another order, the Grandmontines, lived in communities of no more than 12. They believed in no excess and a self-sustaining community, which lived on what it grew. This idea of sustainability and self-sufficiency is popular again today.
Monastic houses managed their land, livestock, mineral rights and waterways. Monasteries also maintained detailed records to pass down knowledge to those that came after them.
These medieval monastic communities also exercised considerable influence over the ecology of their estates, using land and resources carefully.

The valley of the Rie (now Rye) in North Yorkshire, the home of Rievaulx Abbey, is a good example of managed woodlands. It was coppiced and used as foraging grounds for pigs over many years of monastic stewardship. Terracing made the land more usable in the valley. Water channelling ensured sanitation as well as supplying the fulling mill, to help make textiles and clothing, and for the tanning vats, containers used to treat animal skins to make leather.

In Durham monks from the Cathedral Priory were at the heart of a change in the path of the river Wear. Evidence of this emerged in 2009 when heavy rain caused the ancient river’s route to come to light. It appears that the river’s course had been changed in medieval times to prevent the wooded peninsula of Durham from turning into an island.

A wealth of evidence survives showing just how important gardens and land were to medieval monasteries. While herbals and other historical literature show just how carefully monks used plants in everyday life, many of those ideas, such as sustainability, self-sufficiency and finding spirituality in green spaces, have been absorbed into modern gardening books and are embraced by gardeners today.

articles.title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
articles.author: Tara Deans, Associate Professor of Biomedical Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “The Last of Us,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “SpongeBob SquarePants.”

These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close.

I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.

Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making.
The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus, Ophiocordyceps, which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”

The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin.

Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip. After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again.

How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers, but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.

The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus, showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it.

Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved.

That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus.
Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior.

The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa, uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it.

Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed.

Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.

Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.
Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. Toxoplasma gondii can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats.

While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even become attracted to cat odors. This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.

These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator.

There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.

So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them.
Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.

articles.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky - radio telescopes could help find where these ‘ghost particles’ originate
articles.author: Yjan Gordon, Instructor of Physics, University of Wisconsin-Whitewater
paras: Neutrinos are funny little particles that weigh almost nothing, making them one of the universe’s most elusive building blocks. They can come from objects as mundane as bananas and as exotic as supernovas – the exploding death throes of massive stars. Most neutrinos stream through space and pass through the Earth without interacting with anything.

An experiment called IceCube, built to detect these “ghost particles” emitted from astrophysical events, just won a Nobel Prize. As a physicist, I’m interested in figuring out where the neutrinos IceCube detects come from. A study that my colleagues and I published in October 2026 suggests that we could potentially use radio telescopes to answer this question.

Even though these telescopes can’t see neutrinos, we can use their data to match up IceCube’s detections with their potential sources out in space. Knowing which types of objects produce neutrinos can tell astronomers about the physics occurring within those objects.
The shy nature of neutrinos

Most particles interact with the universe through a fundamental force of nature called electromagnetism. It’s the force that powers the phone, tablet or computer that you may be reading this article on. It drives all the chemistry responsible for life, and it’s responsible for the light your eyes can see.

What makes neutrinos odd is that they don’t interact with the universe through electromagnetism. Instead, they interact with the universe via a force that physicists call the weak interaction. This force only acts over distances smaller than the inside of an atomic nucleus; as such, they must pass very, very close to the centers of atoms in order to interact – otherwise they just fly right through. That makes them very difficult to detect – but not impossible.
Scientists have been able to detect neutrinos from space – called astrophysical neutrinos – since the 1960s. These typically come from our Sun and, in at least one case, from a supernova.

Over the past decade or so, researchers at the appropriately named IceCube Observatory have used the South Pole’s Antarctic ice as a neutrino telescope. The densely packed ice gives neutrinos many opportunities to interact with water molecules, and detectors can see radiation from those interactions when they do occur.

Even so, neutrinos really are one of nature’s most introverted particles, and it takes time for any of the ice molecules to get lucky and interact with a neutrino. But, with enough time, it eventually happens. And with more time, it happens again. The more time you give it, the more interactions you see, and the more neutrinos you detect.

IceCube has used this approach to detect astrophysical neutrinos that are hundreds of thousands of times more energetic than those previously seen. The discovery of these high-energy astrophysical neutrinos has opened up a new window on our universe.

The same property that makes them difficult to detect – namely their reluctance to interact with their surroundings – also makes them an effective way to see high-energy processes in places that light can’t penetrate. The problem is we’re not sure where they all come from.
Where could astrophysical neutrinos come from?

Scientists do have some ideas about their origin, of course. Quasars – objects where matter is being ripped apart by black holes millions of times more massive than our Sun – seem to be likely candidates. In 2017, IceCube detected a neutrino that appeared to come from the direction of a quasar, known as TXS 0506+056, at the same time that a telescope detected an outburst of gamma radiation from that same object.

That finding is interesting because the processes that produce neutrinos – namely the decay of subatomic particles – should also produce high-energy electromagnetic radiation – namely gamma rays. So scientists expect neutrino sources to also produce gamma-ray outbursts.

However, TXS 0506+056 is just one object. It may not be representative of where most high-energy neutrinos come from. So far, there’s been little evidence of a more general relationship between gamma-ray outbursts and neutrino detections. But gamma rays can be easily obscured.

Much like the lead apron that the technician taking your X-ray at the hospital wears to protect themselves from the radiation, dust and gas that gathers near a supermassive black hole can block gamma rays from ever reaching Earth.

However, another form of electromagnetic radiation that’s invisible to gamma-ray telescopes – radio waves – are not so easily shielded. Using telescopes that look at radio waves from space may provide scientists an alternate way to see what’s going on.

Beginning in 2017, the Very Large Array in New Mexico began tracking how radio emissions from space change in brightness over time, a project known as the Very Large Array Sky Survey, or VLASS for short. My team and I recently showed that most of the objects seen by VLASS with fluctuating radio emissions are quasars, of the same type that IceCube previously saw producing neutrinos.
Interestingly, when we compared the times that IceCube detected neutrinos with the times when objects spotted by VLASS experienced flares of radio emission, there appeared to be a correlation.

Put another way, when an astrophysical neutrino is detected by IceCube, there is a radio source brightening in the same part of the sky, more often than you’d expect from random chance. These radio flares seem to only be associated with about 13% of the astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube, which means we still can’t account for the origin of the majority of astrophysical neutrinos. However, more than 90% of the radio outbursts potentially associated with neutrinos aren’t seen at all by our gamma-ray telescopes.
If the neutrino’s source of origin is hidden at gamma-ray wavelengths, but not at radio wavelengths, then radio telescopes could become an essential tool in neutrino astronomy.

At the moment, the signal we’re seeing is intriguing, even tantalizing. But there’s about a 1-in-30 chance of getting the results we see even if there’s no correlation between neutrinos and radio flares. Those are roughly the same odds as tossing a coin five times and getting heads every time: unlikely, but not impossible.

Scientists are far more comfortable when the odds of a result being due to random chance are closer to one in a million – the same as getting heads 20 times in a row. To confirm if what we’re seeing is real or not, we need more observations. We expect to have those in the next few years.
One thing is for sure, though: It’s an exciting time to be studying the origins of astrophysical neutrinos, and it looks like radio astronomers may have a big role to play.

articles.title: Philadelphia’s Academy of Natural Sciences just closed – a blow for budding young scientists like me
articles.author: Lili Mei Granda Argianas, Ph.D. Student in Physics, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: When I was a freshman in college at Villanova University outside Philadelphia, I visited the Academy of Natural Sciences for the first time.

My friends who were Philly natives were my tour guides, and I was inspired by their passion for the exhibits. I listened not only to the facts they shared about the museum, but also their childhood stories surrounding it.

As a kid, I remember going to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City and looking up at the massive dinosaur displays. I wondered how creatures as big as those used to walk the same ground as me. My favorite exhibit was the Hall of Ocean Life, where behind the staircase you see a dark, unlit diorama of a giant squid attached to a sperm whale.
The museum gave my curiosity a place to grow.

Now, as a Ph.D. student in physics, I research black holes, with the goal of one day becoming a professor and mentoring students. I was shocked when I heard the news that the Academy of Natural Sciences would be closing.
Over 200 years of hands-on science

Founded in 1812, the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia is the country’s oldest natural science museum. For two centuries, it has played a vital role in scientific research, education and public engagement. The academy’s research centered heavily on biodiversity, evolution, paleontology and environmental science. In 2011, Drexel University acquired the academy and manages its endowment.

The academy had offered a range of experiences, from the Dinosaur Hall to its butterfly garden, and provided generations of visitors with opportunities to explore science beyond classrooms and textbooks.

On Sept. 1, 2026, however, Drexel University abruptly announced that the museum would close by the end of the month, citing financial difficulties and declining attendance. The last day it was open to visitors was Sept. 27, 2026.

Critics of the decision to close are rallying to “Save the Academy” and reopen it. Even members of the Philadelphia City Council expressed surprise that they had not been approached for support before the closing was announced.

The William Penn Foundation offered to cover operating subsidies for at least another year, potentially giving the academy time to explore a sustainable future. However, the museum remains closed for now, and Drexel maintains it needs a long-term financial solution. At a hearing on Oct. 26 that lasted nearly four hours, Philadelphia City Council members tried to understand why the museum closed and what Drexel would need to reopen it. The hearing is scheduled to resume on Nov. 16.
Cultivating future scientists
While museums may be viewed simply as sites for school field trips or family outings, their impact extends far beyond entertainment.

Natural science museums preserve scientific history through linking the past to future generations, supporting research and introducing young people to subjects they might otherwise never encounter. Philly kids who visited the academy could experience different ecosystems, from the snowy lands of the bobcat to rainforests home to giant monkeys. These dioramas are a snapshot in time that allow children to cultivate their own imagination and passions.

Not everyone has the opportunity to attend college or pursue a career in STEM. Museums help close that gap, giving families, students and children a chance to experience science firsthand – something that textbooks, social media and even classrooms sometimes cannot do.

Thinking back to my own childhood, I can pinpoint how my academic interests were fostered through museums, whether gazing up at galaxies at the Hayden Planetarium or sleeping under the belly of the blue whale in the Hall of Ocean Life. I was able to talk to real scientists in careers I dreamed to achieve, and I was told it was possible for me.
These experiences were integral to my becoming a first-generation college student and pursuing a career in academia. They made a career in science feel tangible rather than mystical or intimidating.

articles.title: Chemists create disappearing tattoos: here’s the science behind how they work
articles.author: Miriam O'Duill, Associate Professor of Chemistry, University of Nottingham
paras: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.

Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder have developed invisible tattoo ink than can be revealed with a UV torch and stays visible until switched off with white light. They have published their research in the journal Matter & Light.
They created different motifs with this ink ranging from a lantern that reveals its light when activated, to multicoloured scales like those in the much-loved children’s book The Rainbow Fish.

The pigments used in these inks are so-called photochromic dyes (from the Greek “photos”, which means “light” and “chroma”, which means “colour”). In other words, they are compounds that change colour when exposed to light. These dyes have been used for years in colour-changing sunglasses.
Light carries energy, and photochromic compounds are designed in such a way that this energy is enough to cause a chemical change that alters the shape and therefore the properties of the molecule.

In the case of the “invisible” tattoo ink, two or three seconds of bright ultraviolet (UV) light is enough to form a new ring in the dye molecule, which switches a colourless pigment to a coloured one. A variety of colours are available depending on the exact structure of the molecule.

A blast of bright white light reverses the reaction, breaking the ring and turning the colour off again. For a long time, the challenge with this chemistry was that the coloured form of the dye was relatively unstable and quickly reverted to the more stable, colourless form – especially at higher temperatures.

Another issue was fatigue: after a certain number of on-off cycles, the dyes degraded and took on a permanent coloured hue. Have you ever bought transition lens sunglasses and noticed that they became less effective over time? This is due to the same deterioration of photochromic compounds in the lenses. But thanks to recent research efforts, remarkably stable dyes have been designed that reliably hold their colour for months and can undergo over 10,000 activation and deactivation cycles without degrading.

Carson Bruns’ team at the University of Colorado Boulder showed that these pigments could be formulated into tattoo inks by encapsulating them in poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), a polymer approved for medical use in bone cement, dentures and intraocular lenses. This family of inks is known as PhotoTat.

So, when will you be able to get one of these switchable tattoos? A red pigment was already launched in 2024 under the name Magic Ink by Colorado-based biotech company Hyprskn. A 2 millilitre (ml) vial will set you back £77, which is about 100 times more expensive than regular tattoo ink due to the specialised dyes and formulation process required. The ink is fully compliant with the EU’s Reach (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) safety regulations.

Now, Bruns’ research team has developed three more PhotoTat inks – blue, magenta and yellow – that can combine into 16 other colours. “So far,” Bruns says, “the only person who’s tested this ink is me. I actually have hundreds of these tattoos on my legs now and they’ve all gone really well.”

Some challenges remain though: direct sunlight contains enough UV radiation to activate the tattoos unless they are protected by sunscreen. Indoor light will slowly switch them off over a period of several days.

In addition, the blue ink currently degrades after only 10–100 activations, leaving a permanent, purple-coloured mark. Most importantly, the inks need to undergo thorough toxicity and safety testing before they can be rolled out to tattoo shops for general use, which will likely take several years. Don’t get your hopes up just yet about your new “business during the day, party at night” look.

When Hyprskn launched Magic Ink, the reception in the tattoo community was mixed. While some tattoo enthusiasts viewed it as a revolutionary creative tool, others thought it was an overpriced gimmick. Bruns does not only see his photochromic tattoo inks as fashion accessories, however.

He also envisages medical applications, for example for patients who need permanent skin markings to guide radiation therapy or identify sites for biopsies. Bruns argues that these markings “become a permanent reminder of a traumatic experience” which can be mitigated by making the tattoo invisible once it is no longer needed in a clinical setting.

articles.title: How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles
articles.author: Philip Mannion, Professor of Palaeobiology, UCL
paras: My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza.

Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle.

Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament.

Studying the anatomy of the skeletons of living and fossil gavials has given us a better understanding of the group’s evolution in recent years. CT scans have enabled us to look inside their skulls, giving us a window into their brains and sensory systems.
This has revealed new anatomical information that helps differentiate species, and has allowed us to infer aspects of the biology and ecology of some of the extinct species.

For example, in an extinct group of crocodile relatives known to have lived entirely in the ocean, other researchers found thickening of the outer wall of their inner ear to cope with the higher pressures seen at ocean depths. My colleagues and I have found similar evidence for a marine lifestyle in some fossil gavials. This ability to live in the ocean was lost in living species, which are restricted to rivers and lakes.

Several of the gavial fossils we have been studying from Africa and Europe were first reported in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and they were often described as species of Tomistoma, i.e. closely related to Tomistoma schlegelii, one of the two living species of gavials. Our previous work and that of others has shown that some of these extinct species are not closely related to Tomistoma, with new names given for some of them. However, many of these historically described species remain neglected. Led by my former PhD student, Paul Burke, now a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, along with colleagues from Egypt and Germany, we re-examined one of these species in a new study.

In the 1920s, several fossils were collected from northeastern Egypt. These were found in a limestone rock, known as the Mokattam Formation, that had formed 45 million years ago in a shallow marine environment when sea levels were higher. This region was submerged at this time. These fossils, including a nearly complete skull, were described in 1927 as belonging to Tomistoma, because of their superficial resemblance to the living species, Tomistoma schlegelii.
However, aided by the use of CT scanning, our team was able to identify several anatomical differences, including the presence of raised rims around the eye sockets, which are absent in Tomistoma.

The Mokattam Formation already has a legacy: 4,500 years ago, these rocks were used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. The gavial skull shares more than this origin story though. Just as the Sphinx is famously missing the tip of its nose, the fossil is also missing the tip of its snout. This coincidence led us to name the new crocodile Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian falcon-headed god Heru (also known as Horus), who is often thought to be the inspiration for the iconic Sphinx.

Both northern Africa and southern Europe hosted a high diversity of gavials (and other crocodiles) during much of the last 80 million years, with these species thriving in the shallow, marine environments that covered much of the Mediterranean region at the time.

Unlike living gavials, it is likely that some of these species could cross oceans. This diversity appears to have persisted through the devastating mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, and probably fluctuated during alternating warmer and cooler intervals over the next 60 million years, tied to higher and lower sea levels, respectively.

However, crocodiles disappeared from the Mediterranean region approximately 6 million years ago and never returned. Their demise coincides with an event known as the Messinian salinity crisis, when the Mediterranean essentially dried up as a result of being sealed off from the Atlantic Ocean. As the seawater became increasingly salty with the heightened evaporation of water, it would have become ever more intolerable to the animals inhabiting it, even those usually able to live in saltwater, leading to the loss of crocodiles and many other species.

The signature of this event can still be observed today, with the Mediterranean Sea still much saltier than the oceans, and crocodiles entirely absent from this region. The remaining living gavials live far away from the Mediterranean, but the loss of the adaptations that would allow them to live in saltwater means that they would not be able to survive there regardless.

Rapid and extreme changes in temperature, sea level, and aridification are critical components of the current climate emergency, and events such as the Messinian salinity crisis show that they can have a lasting impact on biodiversity, spanning millions of years.
Philip Mannion receives funding from The Royal Society and UK Research and Innovation.

articles.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
articles.author: Calli Tzani, Reader in Psychology, Cyberpsychology Research Network Co-Director and ADM Forensic Editor, University of Huddersfield
paras: Social media doesn’t necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behaviour is justified.
We are addressing that imbalance, with our framework, the Algorithmic Trait Amplification, or ATA, with particular regard to narcissism.

Narcissism runs on a spectrum. At the far end is narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis. But many people have milder narcissistic traits – a strong need for admiration, a habit of overrating their own importance, struggling to take criticism, little empathy. That said, some traits such as healthy ambition and assertiveness are beneficial.
People who have these traits, which are common, are especially drawn to social media and platforms built around status and approval from others.

For years we have been studying online behaviour and the affect of social media upon relationships; including how psychopathy shows up in romantic relationships and how TikTok shapes young women’s attraction to dangerous partners. That work, combined with what psychology already knows on how narcissistic people operate online, how algorithms chase engagement, and what personality change requires led us to a realisation. The algorithmic loop process may slowly strengthen an inflated, entitled self-image.
These are the five steps over which ATA predicts that social media will heighten narcissistic traits.
Stage 1: The engagement hook

Someone with narcissistic traits tends to react strongly to content that matches their self-image. Winning. Status. Being special. Always being right. Most of us have some version of a For You content feed. But for people high in these traits, the pull is more powerful. Such content fulfils a narcissist’s higher need for validation.

Social media recommendation systems are designed to keep us engaged but they cannot tell whether the content is good for us. They only measure whether it holds our attention. Our reactions become instructions: give this person more of this, feed the loop.

For example, a user rewatches a video about how “strong personalities intimidate weak people”. The app notices and fills the feed with content about cutting off “toxic” friends and refusing to apologise. Every video tells them the problem is everyone else. And they agree. So, they watch more.

Audit studies of online recommendation systems show that feeds narrow in proportion to how selectively a user engages. Someone low in narcissistic traits engages more evenly in different types of content. Someone high in these traits engages hard and narrow and the algorithm obliges.
Stage 3: The mirror oracle
We call this the echo algorithm, after the Greek myth of Narcissus. The nymph Echo can only repeat what is said to her. She cannot challenge or answer back.

Social media algorithms are the same. Over time, the user unknowingly builds a mirror: more praise, more validation, more self-image inflation. And the worst part for narcissistic users is that the feed feels like the world agrees with them. Objective. External. Almost all-knowing. But it is an oracle that they trained themselves, to say exactly what they wanted to hear.
Stage 4: Challenge disappears

Psychologists explain that personality change, in all of us, depends on corrective emotional experiences. These are moments that contradict your self-image in a way you cannot ignore. Or as we call them, uncomfortable moments of truth. They are also how people with narcissistic traits change. These moments help us grow. Take them away, and the traits they would have challenged only get stronger.

Content that challenges the narcissist gets less engagement than content that flatters them. Therefore, challenging content and moments of truths slowly vanishes from the feed – an unplanned algorithmic side-effect of platforms’ aim to chase users’ attention.
Stage 5: The loop feeds itself
Fed a diet of constant validation, narcissistic traits may intensify. Stronger traits produce stronger reactions, thus producing an ever more perfect mirror within the loop.

Psychologists don’t agree on whether overall levels of narcissism are on the rise. Some psychologists say it is, while others have found no change. So the argument is not settled. But psychology researchers do agree that narcissistic traits correlate with heavier, more problematic social media use and that the expression of narcissistic behaviour is more visible online. Rising or not, our model predicts that for people who already have these traits, the algorithm may be turning up the volume.

Working with narcissistic clients is already considered one of the hardest jobs in psychology. These clients often experience honest feedback as an attack. On one hand, progress depends on carefully managed moments of challenge, built up over sessions. And many clients never get that far: around two-thirds of people diagnosed with narcissistic personality disorder drop out of therapy early. Change is possible, but only for those who stay.

On the other, their phone, trained on years of their own reactions, may offer a world that reflects them at their best, agrees with their grievances and doesn’t challenge. Their therapist may only have an hour a week with them, while the algorithm gets anytime the person picks up their phone.

Our framework may explain why so many people believe narcissism is on the rise: the behaviour is more visible, because the loop rewards it. The algorithm has been running its own experiment on all of us and we wonder, what else has it been intensifying?

articles.title: We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?
articles.author: Kristen Skruber, Assistant Professor of Biology, Gonzaga University
paras: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.

Organisms can adapt to survive in a wide variety of conditions, from salty water to extreme heat or cold and changing climates. Most eukaryotic organisms that have been studied with cell types similar to our own live at temperatures close to those of the human body, with an average of 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius).

Organisms thriving at temperatures higher than this range, known as thermophiles, could help directly answer what effect temperature has on the rules for life. These rules can help scientists learn more about where life could exist. In a study published in September 2026, our research team identified a new thermophile that can survive at hotter conditions than any other previously recorded.
Discovering life at a new extreme

Eukaryotic cells, like the ones found in our bodies, contain organelles like nuclei and mitochondria. Eukaryotic organisms are reported less often than bacteria in extreme conditions, and based on observations from fungi at 140 F (60 C), scientists had theorized that eukaryotic life is not physically possible beyond 143 F (62 C).

In our new study, our team isolated and characterized a unicellular eukaryote, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which is able to reproduce at 145 F (63 C). This finding marks the highest temperature yet recorded for eukaryotic life.
Our team found Incendiamoeba cascadensis in geothermal springs in Lassen Volcanic National Park, in Northern California, but we suspect it might also be found in other geothermal areas worldwide.

Like many amoebae – cells that change shape as they move – Incendiamoeba is a forager. It can move around in search of food and favorable conditions. It actively crawls at 147 F (64 C), but a few degrees more and it will enter a protective hibernation-like state.
What sets thermophiles apart?

While bacteria have been recorded living up to 212 F (100 C), it is unclear why eukaryotic cells are less amenable to high temperatures and other extremes. Many theories abound: Our cells have more protective membranes, including several membranes within each cell, surrounding their organelles. We also have complex molecular machinery that maintains our large genomes, and a dynamic cytoskeleton: a network of proteins that allows our cells to move.

Like other eukaryotes, Incendiamoeba has organelles, an active cytoskeleton and a relatively large genome, so what allows it to persist where others cannot? So far, Incendiamoeba has revealed that we don’t yet know which parts of eukaryotes are generally incompatible with high temperature.

As someone who investigates phenomena at the molecular level, I am always thinking about how molecules move and how motion increases with temperature. At higher temperatures, the velcrolike bonds holding proteins together can unfold, preventing them from performing their vital functions. Eukaryotes have evolved protein helpers called heat shock proteins, which detect protein unfolding and help refold them.

So, could Incendiamoeba simply have more of these helper proteins? Our team found that it does have a large reservoir of heat shock proteins, but making these proteins requires a lot of energy, and they must be folded themselves, so more helper proteins probably isn’t the full answer.

Incendiamoeba also has a unique set of protein building blocks that are good at holding proteins together. Yet this composition may only make up for the fact that proteins degrade more easily with increasing temperature.

We can look at Incendiamoeba’s genes, which turn on – or up – when temperature rises. Many of these genes are unknown. It is possible that one of these mystery genes is the key to its ability to withstand high temperatures. However, it is more likely, and in my mind, much more interesting, that there exists a symphony of small changes this organism has evolved, which confer its unique abilities.
By investigating Incendiamoeba and finding others like it, we can determine those changes and learn about the key principles for how life works on our environmentally diverse planet.
Kristen Skruber receives funding from the M.J. Murdock Charitable Trust.

articles.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
articles.author: Shannon Roberts, Associate Professor of Industrial Engineering, UMass Amherst
paras: Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes in Texas and California. Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy and lessen transit times.

Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs.
I am an engineer who studies human factors and transportation safety, and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time.

Fully automated trucks, which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, use a combination of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. Torc, one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.

Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping assistance systems indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by optimizing acceleration and braking, and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit convoy or platoon. Driverless trucks could reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.

Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing driver shortage. Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, improving job satisfaction among drivers.
Weather and work zones are hard to navigate
The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions and alongside unpredictable drivers.

Automated trucks require sensors, radars and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem for all automated vehicles, including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, only operates driverless cars in areas that get no snow.

Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines is difficult to handle. Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to avoid these areas. And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars at a higher rate than they do cars piloted by people.
Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications.

For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is operating large freight trucks on I-45, a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are delivering sand to industrial sites in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights and elements of city traffic.
Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction or exited the market.

In 2023, Embark, TuSimple and Locomotion closed down. Waymo began to focus solely on cars. Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a few dedicated routes between two large cities or manufacturing sites.
Drivers and trucks that work together
In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver.

The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile” – the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.

Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that human-machine interfaces that communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles will be key. For example, a screen or heads-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over.

Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called automation bias could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. Algorithmic bias could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.

The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.

Shannon Roberts receives funding from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, National Science Foundation, NYSEARCH, Sloan Foundation, and US Department of Transportation. She has previously received funding from Belron, GM, and Toyota Collaborative Safety Research Center.

articles.title: England needs 120% of normal rainfall to come out of drought this winter – storms won’t fix that yet
articles.author: Hannah Cloke, Regius Professor of Meteorology and Climate Science, University of Reading
paras: Storm Austen and Storm Boelo swept across the UK in quick succession. Rain lashed windows, river levels rose and the clocks went back. It feels like winter has arrived all at once.

Yet most of England and Wales are still in drought. Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset and Sussex are in severe drought, the highest level the Environment Agency can declare. South-west and south-east England have had their driest April to September in over 100 years.

But how can this be when it is cold, dark and pouring with rain? Drought tightens or loosens its grip over months, not just a few days. It will be the rainy or dry nature of the months ahead that will decide whether the drought ends, or more worryingly, if it stays into next summer.
Winter should fill the tank

Summer droughts grab the headlines and public attention. When we have a dry period over the summer it’s everywhere, with brown lawns, hosepipe bans and cracked reservoir beds. But winter is when the UK refills its water stores.

Between October and March, with shorter and colder days, less water evaporates and plants drink far less, so rain finally has the chance to refill our reservoirs. Rain can soak deep into the ground to top up groundwater, the water held in chalk and sandstone rocks beneath our feet, like a giant sponge. Groundwater supplies much of the drinking water in southern and eastern England, but it fills slowly, over months and years.

Think of it like a bank account. A hot summer is a big splurge with lots of withdrawals. But a dry winter means the deposits needed to repay that spending never arrive. That’s why a dry winter can do more damage to our water supplies than a heatwave.

This year the account is badly overdrawn. Southern England has just had its driest April to September in more than a century, alongside record summer heat. The Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor, which supplies around 400,000 people, was full in March, after an extremely wet winter. Then the weather shifted from wetter than normal to dryer than normal. By October, water levels at Wimbleball were down to about 13%.
How unusual is a winter drought?

Droughts that carry on into winter are rare in the UK. Usually the autumn rain arrives, soil gets wetter and water stores recover by Christmas. Every instinct suggests that a stormy autumn should fix things.

In the 2010 to 2012 drought, two dry winters in a row left groundwater in south and east England so low that hosepipe bans came in during spring 2012. Then the wettest April on record arrived, and parts of the country swung from drought to flood within weeks.
What stands out now is how quickly droughts are stacking up. This is the third drought in England in five years. The stores barely have time to recover before the next one begins.

England and Wales can be in drought and experience flooding simultaneously. After months of dry weather it takes a lot of rain to wet the ground all the way through. Storms such as Boelo and Austen bring bursts of heavy rain. Drains are overwhelmed and rivers rise quickly, sometimes spilling out onto their floodplains. But the reservoirs and groundwater that supply our taps respond far more slowly, and need lots of water to fill up. So the type of winter rains make a big difference.

Floods can hit fast. But the key parts of the water cycle are slow. Rain has to wet the soil all the way through before it can trickle down into the rock, and groundwater can take months to respond. The Environment Agency estimates England needs around 120% of normal rainfall between September and April for every area to come out of drought. We would need half a year with consistently more rain than we would expect at this time of year to break this drought.
If rain falls short across the whole winter, then England could start next summer in drought, with even less room for manoeuvre.
Will winter droughts become more common?

But climate scientists don’t expect there will be a dry winter every year, either now or in decades ahead as fossil fuel burning continues to heat the planet. Climate projections suggest UK winters will get wetter on average. But averages can hide the danger.

Summers heated by the burning of fossil fuels dry out the soil and drain reservoirs faster, leaving a bigger hole for winter to fill. Winter rain is increasingly arriving in heavy bursts that are harder to capture and more likely to flood. And natural swings in the weather will still deliver dry winters from time to time. Put those together and the chance of a drought rolling into winter, or across two winters, goes up. This is a trend that will keep getting worse as long as we keep heating the planet.
Preparing starts with how we think about water. It is precious, not endless. Yet we have built a system that lets a wet winter rush away to the sea, then rations what is left through a dry summer.

As with other parts of the UK’s water system, we are paying the price now for years of chronic underinvestment. Water companies need to move much faster on fixing leaks, which still waste billions of litres every day. New reservoirs are being planned in England, which will help deliver more storage. But they will take more than a decade to build, cost billions of pounds, and cannot be the whole solution.

There is also a low-tech local answer, that would need regulation and a programme of retrofitting to make a big difference. Rainwater harvesting and water reuse in new and existing homes, sustainable drainage in our towns, and encouraging wetlands and floodplains that hold water like a sponge.
Changes to our landscape and homes can help prevent both problems.
Each of us can help. Take shorter showers, ask your water company about a meter and and fit a water butt to catch rain for the garden. These habits add up.
Autumn storms have started to replenish water reserves, but it’s not the finish line. We also need to get ahead of what is likely to happen in years to come.

Hannah Cloke advises the Environment Agency, the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts, the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, local and national governments and humanitarian agencies on the forecasting and warning of natural hazards. She is a fellow of the European Centre for Medium-range Weather Forecasts. Her research is funded by the UKRI Engineering & Physical Sciences Research Council, the UKRI Natural Environment Research Council, the European Commission and the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.

articles.title: The UK wants ‘AI sovereignty’ to cut its reliance on foreign tech – here’s how that can be achieved
articles.author: Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
paras: The UK government wants to grow the country’s native AI industry to reduce its dependence on systems made by foreign companies.
In the Budget on October 28, Chancellor John Healey announced more money – £60 million – for the national Sovereign AI Fund to support promising UK AI companies.

The government launched the fund in April 2026, committing £500 million at the time to boost the UK’s AI capability. Based in the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), it operates much like a government backed venture capital fund.

But this unit offers more than money. Companies can gain access to some of the UK’s most powerful AI supercomputers, including Isambard-AI, alongside research support and opportunities to work with the government.

The UK government initiatives are part of a wider global push towards sovereign AI. This term refers to countries strengthening their ability to develop and use the AI technologies they rely on while retaining greater control over them. There is concern about the risks of dependence on foreign suppliers – and the potential disruption to UK infrastructure if something were to happen to one of those suppliers.
But what does sovereign AI mean in practice – and can the UK learn anything from what’s going on elsewhere in the world?

For some, sovereignty means controlling everything needed to develop and run AI. For others, it means building domestic AI models or keeping data within national borders. A recent analysis published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace shows how complex this can be.
AI depends on computer chips, data, electricity, skilled workers, internet connections, and cybersecurity. A country may control some of these while depending on foreign suppliers for others.
In practice, four ideas tend to be bundled together. The first is ownership: who owns the chips, data centres, and models? The second is jurisdiction: whose laws apply and where is the data held?

The third is capability: can a country build, adapt, and run AI itself? The fourth is resilience: can essential services continue if a supplier withdraws access? Many disagreements about sovereign AI concern which of these ideas matters most.
The Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a US think tank, tracks government-backed sovereign AI projects. In January 2023, it recorded just one project.

By mid-2026, that number had risen to 184 projects across 67 countries. These figures show how quickly interest in sovereign AI has grown globally. However, they count projects, not whether those projects have succeeded.

Countries are making different choices about where to invest. India, for example, has focused on building domestic computing capacity, promoting the development of AI models and setting up national datasets for “training” AI models. Its IndiaAI Mission has deployed around 38,000 graphics processing units (GPUs) – specialised processors used to develop and run AI – to boost computing power for developers.
Other Indian initiatives include BharatGen AI, a multilingual AI model, and AIKosh, a national platform to provide startups and researchers with access to anonymised training data.

According to the same report by CNAS, most countries focus on just one or two layers of the AI stack – the collection of technologies and infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI systems. Only a handful of jurisdictions, such as India, South Korea, the UK, and Taiwan, have operational programmes covering computing infrastructure, models, and data. Ghana and South Africa, meanwhile, have launched projects focused on expanding domestic AI computing capacity.
Sovereign and also dependent?

While some nations are making strides towards sovereign AI, almost every country relies on foreign AI technology to some extent. Rather than developing models from scratch, many adapt existing – or base – models developed abroad. According to CNAS, around three-fifths of the foreign base models identified in the projects it tracks come from the US.

A 2026 report by researchers from the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) at Georgetown University, Washington DC, highlights the risks of foreign technology supply chains. Trade restrictions and geopolitical tensions can disrupt access, particularly to advanced computer chips, which are produced by a small number of specialised suppliers. But dependence is not the whole story.

Researchers at Stanford University in California have argued that sovereignty is better understood as managing AI dependencies rather than eliminating them. Their report underlines the fact that supporting domestic companies and adopting open-source technologies can widen the available choices.

Diversifying foreign technology suppliers is another option. For example, the CNAS report identifies projects in Egypt, Singapore, Thailand, Uganda, and the UAE using Alibaba’s Qwen models, developed in China. Many Qwen models are open source and offer an alternative to those developed in Silicon Valley.

Switzerland takes a different approach. Its Apertus model is a Swiss-developed large language model that openly shares information about its training data, code, and development process. In the Swiss canton of Ticino, it powers an in-house translation service for sensitive government documents without relying on commercial AI providers. The priority here is greater control over how the technology is used, rather than simply choosing the most powerful AI model.
Less a switch, more a dial

There are limits, however. As the Stanford researchers point out, commercial products marketed as “sovereign AI” may still rely on foreign providers. Even models that can be freely adapted still need chips, electricity, and skilled people.

If sovereignty means owning every part of the AI technology stack, almost no country qualifies. But if it means maintaining control when circumstances change, the picture looks different. What matters is whether countries have meaningful choices.

Can they switch suppliers without disrupting essential services? Can they enforce their own laws and adapt AI technologies to local languages, priorities, and needs? These questions reveal more about a country’s sovereignty than simply counting how many chips, data centres, or AI models it owns.

Sovereignty then looks less like a switch and more like a dial. For the UK, the real test will be whether its Sovereign AI Unit gives the country greater freedom to choose and adapt AI technologies as the programme develops.
“Sovereign AI” will probably continue to mean different things to different governments. But the label itself tells us little about how much control a country actually has.
